tldr: EmotiCrafter generates an image from a free-text prompt plus a pair of continuous Valence-Arousal (V-A) values, so the same scene can be rendered with finely graded emotions instead of a handful of emotion labels. It works by shifting the prompt's text features toward an emotional version before they condition Stable Diffusion XL. In experiments and user studies it conveys the intended emotion more accurately and more smoothly than existing techniques.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: Free-text prompt + Valence and Arousal values in [-3, 3]

facts.label: Backbone
facts.value: Stable Diffusion XL with a GPT-2-based emotion injection transformer

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Neutral/emotional prompt pairs built from 39,843 V-A-annotated images

facts.label: Evaluation
facts.value: 4 baselines, 3,300 images per method, 2 user studies (20 participants)

contributions: Defines the continuous emotional image content generation (C-EICG) task and presents EmotiCrafter, the first model dedicated to it.

Introduces an emotion-embedding network that fuses continuous V-A values with text-prompt features, which are then injected into Stable Diffusion XL through cross-attention to control both content and emotion.
Proposes a loss function that amplifies the difference between neutral and emotional text features and weights samples by the V-A distribution to counter data imbalance.
Builds an emotional prompts dataset in which each neutral prompt is paired with an emotional prompt that keeps the same core meaning but expresses the emotion of a given V-A pair.

sections.heading: Motivation
paragraphs: Emotions shape memory and comprehension, so content creators increasingly use them to engage audiences. Yet while visual emotion analysis is extensive, generating emotionally rich images has received far less attention.

EmoGen pioneered domain-free emotional image generation from an emotion tag such as "happy" or "sad". This leaves two gaps: content is hard to control without a text prompt, and discrete tags cannot capture nuanced emotions, especially since psychologists have not agreed on a fixed set of emotion categories.

EmotiCrafter instead adopts the Valence-Arousal model, a well-known continuous emotion model. Valence measures pleasantness (negative to positive) and Arousal measures intensity (calm to excited), each on a [-3, 3] scale. A continuous space supports smooth transitions and subtle shifts, such as moving from "bored" to "tired", that discrete labels cannot express.

figures.caption: The Valence-Arousal model: emotions are positioned in a two-dimensional space spanned by valence (negative to positive) and arousal (low to high).

sections.heading: Model Architecture
paragraphs: Given a prompt and a pair of V-A values, a prompt encoder first turns the prompt into a neutral prompt feature. An emotion-embedding network then transforms this feature into an emotional prompt feature that reflects the requested V-A values. That feature conditions Stable Diffusion XL through its cross-attention mechanism to produce the final image.
The network predicts the residual between emotional and neutral prompt features and adds it back to the neutral feature, preserving the original textual context while infusing emotion.
bullets: V-A Encoder: two separate multilayer perceptrons map the valence and arousal values to a V-feature and an A-feature.

Emotion Injection Transformer: a modified GPT-2 that projects the neutral prompt feature into its hidden space (with positional embedding) and passes it through 12 Emotion Injection Blocks. The causal mask used for next-token prediction is removed.

Emotion Injection Block: self-attention followed by two cross-attention layers, which inject the V-feature and then the A-feature, and a feed-forward network, each with LayerNorm and a residual connection.
Output projection: a linear layer and LayerNorm map the final hidden state back to the SDXL prompt feature space as the predicted residual.

figures.caption: Method overview. (a) Images annotated with V-A values are paired with GPT-4-generated neutral and emotional prompts. (b.1) The emotion-embedding network embeds V-A values into textual features; (b.2) a specialized loss enhances emotional expression. The output conditions the image generator.
Structure of an Emotion Injection Block. The V-feature and A-feature are injected into the hidden state through successive cross-attention modules.

sections.heading: Loss Function
paragraphs: The network is trained to match a scaled target emotional prompt feature, with a loss that combines two strategies. Together they aim to make emotional changes more pronounced while compensating for the uneven distribution of V-A values in the training data.
bullets: Scaled residual learning: the target residual between emotional and neutral prompt features is enlarged by a factor α, set to 1.5 based on the ablation study.

V-A density weighting: each sample's loss is weighted inversely to the density of training samples at its V-A position. The density is estimated with Gaussian kernel density estimation, with bandwidth chosen by Silverman's rule of thumb.

sections.heading: Dataset & Training
paragraphs: The training set pairs neutral and emotional prompts with V-A values. GPT-4 generated the pairs from 39,843 images with human-annotated V-A values drawn from the public OASIS, EMOTIC, and FindingEmo datasets. Neutral prompts give objective descriptions of each image, while emotional prompts emphasize affective attributes such as color, lighting, and texture.

All LLM-generated prompts went through crowd-sourced verification, with disagreements resolved by annotator voting. The emotion-embedding network was trained on two NVIDIA A800 GPUs with AdamW (learning rate 1e-3, weight decay 1e-5) for 200 epochs at batch size 768, which took about 7 to 8 hours.

sections.heading: Experiments
paragraphs: Qualitative results show four capabilities. V-A values can override emotional cues in the prompt, for example rendering "a child in the amusement park" as sad. Discrete emotion categories can be expressed as points in V-A space. Images can be generated from an empty prompt with emotion as the only condition. Emotion can also be controlled finely, in V-A steps of 0.2.

Four baselines inject emotion features through SDXL's UNet cross-attention (IP-Adapter-based), its time embedding, or Textual Inversion placeholders, or have GPT-4 rewrite the prompt according to the V-A values (GPT-4+SDXL). The first three tended to produce nearly identical images regardless of the emotion input. Only EmotiCrafter and GPT-4+SDXL showed clear emotional variation, and GPT-4+SDXL had noticeable discontinuities under extreme V-A values.
bullets: Setup: 3,300 images per method (132 prompts × 5 valence × 5 arousal values).
Emotion accuracy: EmotiCrafter achieved the lowest A-Error (1.828) and V-Error (1.510), compared with 1.860 and 1.517 for GPT-4+SDXL.

Prompt fidelity: CLIPScore was 23.067, below the best baseline (26.566, Time Embedding). The authors attribute this to the inherent trade-off between emotional modulation and strict semantic alignment.
Image quality: CLIP-IQA was 0.881, which the authors report as comparable to the baselines (highest: 0.949, Cross Attention).
Continuity: LPIPS-Continuous was 0.220, compared with 0.361 for GPT-4+SDXL (lower is smoother).

figures.caption: Qualitative comparison with baselines at V-A values of -1.5, 0, and 1.5. Only EmotiCrafter and GPT-4+SDXL clearly reflect emotional variation, and EmotiCrafter's transitions are more continuous.

A 5 × 5 V-A grid (values from -3 to 3) for "A group of people is skiing in a snow hill". EmotiCrafter stays continuous even at extreme values, while GPT-4+SDXL shows discontinuities (e.g., in the V=3 column).

sections.heading: User Study
paragraphs: Two studies with 20 college students compared EmotiCrafter with GPT-4+SDXL. In Study I, participants reordered sets of five images by perceived valence or arousal and estimated each image's values. Ordering accuracy was measured with Kendall's τb, alongside the absolute error of the estimates. In Study II, participants rated 25-image sets spanning V-A values from -3 to +3 on 5-point Likert scales for how well the images followed the V-A changes and how smooth the transitions were.
EmotiCrafter outperformed the baseline on every metric. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showed statistically significant improvements in ranking, error, consistency, and smoothness.
bullets: Ranking consistency (Kendall's τb): arousal 0.759 vs. 0.165; valence 0.887 vs. 0.584.
Estimation error: arousal 1.327 vs. 2.029; valence 0.692 vs. 1.229.
Likert ratings: emotion consistency 4.215 vs. 3.525; emotion smoothness 4.240 vs. 3.195.

figures.caption: User study results comparing EmotiCrafter (Ours) with GPT-4+SDXL (Baseline): V/A ranking, V/A error, and emotion consistency and smoothness (*p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).

sections.heading: Ablation Study
paragraphs: Increasing the scaling factor α lowers CLIPScore, meaning weaker semantic alignment, but also lowers V/A-Error, meaning more accurate emotion. The authors chose α = 1.5 as a trade-off and note that users can adjust it to suit their needs. Removing the density weighting raised V-Error from 1.510 to 1.546 and lowered CLIPScore from 23.067 to 21.977, with A-Error nearly unchanged.

figures.caption: Ablation on "An oil painting shows an astronaut." As α increases, image-prompt similarity decreases while emotional variation increases; density weighting d(v, a) makes emotional changes more accurate.

sections.heading: Limitations & Future Work
bullets: Arousal is harder to control than valence, consistent with prior findings that arousal has lower inter-annotator agreement.
The model often adds human activities that the prompt does not mention, likely because non-human scenes are under-represented in the training data. More diverse non-human scenarios could help.
The model occasionally shifts the prompt's meaning to fit the target emotion. The authors suggest adding a semantic preservation term to the loss.
